name: Hair dye / bleaching hair

lead: Hair dyeing and bleaching change hair colour with chemical colourants or lighteners. Looksmaxxers use them on scalp hair, brows, lashes and facial hair to adjust contrast, cover grey, or make sparse eyebrows and beards look darker and fuller.

The chain is direct: permanent dyes use ammonia and peroxide to open the cuticle and form colour in the hair, and bleach oxidises melanin; semi-permanent and temporary dyes coat or sit under the cuticle and wash out. The chemistry is well documented, and the colour change is visible right after application.

paras: People apply boxed colour at home or have it done at a salon, choosing permanent, semi-permanent or temporary formulas depending on how long they want it to last. Brow and beard tints are usually done as shorter, targeted applications. Bleaching is often followed by toning and conditioning.

Allergy to PPD can cause itching, burning and sores, sometimes delayed, and can be severe. Peroxide bleaching can damage hair and skin. IARC lists some ingredients as mutagenic or carcinogenic, though overall evidence linking dye use to cancer is described as limited and inconsistent. The EU restricts many dye chemicals.

angle.text: You dye or bleach scalp hair, eyebrows, lashes or facial hair to change contrast, cover grey, or make sparse brows and beards look darker and fuller. The colour change is visible straight after application. It is a long-established cosmetic practice.

lead: Hair dyeing and bleaching change the colour of scalp hair, and in looksmaxxing circles also of eyebrows, lashes and facial hair. People use them to match hair colour to skin tone and eye colour, to add or reduce contrast around the face, to cover grey, to make sparse brows or a patchy beard read as darker and fuller, or to move to a different overall look [1][2][3][4]. Wikipedia reports that 50 to 80 percent of women in the United States, Europe and Japan say they have used hair dye, and that US at-home colour sales reached about 4.8 billion dollars in 2024 [3].

Products are classed by permanence. Permanent dyes use an alkaline agent, usually ammonia, and a peroxide developer, and can lighten as well as deposit colour; demi-permanent and semi-permanent dyes deposit colour without lightening and fade over weeks; temporary colour washes out with one shampoo [3]. Bleach lifts colour by oxidising melanin, which is the route to blonde or to vivid shades on dark hair [3].

The main documented harm is allergic contact dermatitis, particularly to para-phenylenediamine (PPD) and related dye intermediates, which is covered by reviews of cosmetic allergy and by trials in sensitised patients [5][6][7][8]. Cancer research on personal hair dye use has produced mixed results: the US National Cancer Institute says it is unknown whether current dye chemicals cause cancer, and IARC classes personal use as not classifiable [9][3].

paras: Hair colouring can be done by a hairdresser or at home. Wikipedia lists the usual motives as covering grey or white hair, creating a specific look, switching to a preferred colour and restoring colour lost to hairdressing processes or sun bleaching [3]. Application techniques fall into off-scalp methods, such as highlighting, lowlighting, balayage, ombre and foiling, and on-scalp methods, such as all-over colour, root touch-ups and block colouring [3].

For looksmaxxers the interest is mostly in matching colour to the face. Forum threads ask which dye best reproduces the darker look a user's hair has when wet, how to go from ginger to black, how to tell whether black or dark brown suits a particular face, and what colour to use around the eyes [10][1][11][2]. A separate thread discusses dye on eyebrows, lashes and facial hair for users with dark hair [4].

Permanent dyes contain ammonia and are mixed with a developer, hydrogen peroxide, which comes in different volumes; the higher the volume, the more natural pigment is lifted, and typical processing is 30 to 45 minutes [3]. Ammonia opens the cuticle so colourant and developer can reach the cortex, where oxidation couples small precursor molecules into larger dye molecules that no longer wash out [3].

Wikipedia describes oxidative dyes as needing a primary intermediate (historically 1,4-diaminobenzene, now usually 2,5-diaminotoluene), a coupler and an oxidant, with the coupler largely setting the final colour [3]. Demi-permanent dyes use a non-ammonia alkaline agent with weaker peroxide, give almost no lightening, cover grey better than semi-permanents and fade over about 20 to 28 shampoos [3].

Semi-permanent dyes use no developer or ammonia, last about 4 to 8 shampoos, and give a more natural, slightly varied shade, but cover grey poorly and may still contain PPD [3]. Temporary rinses, gels, sprays and foams sit on the cuticle and wash out with a single shampoo [3]. Vivid or alternative colours are usually tint only, so they show best on bleached or very light hair [3].

Bleaching oxidises melanin with hydrogen peroxide made alkaline with ammonia, releasing oxygen gas as the pigment breaks down. Home products typically contain about 6 percent peroxide and salon products up to 12 percent [3]. Bleached hair can develop a brassy or yellow cast, which toners and purple shampoo are used to counter [3].

Wikipedia lists henna, indigo, cassia, senna, turmeric and amla among long-used plant dyes, notes that indigo is applied in a colourless leuco form, and describes a 2018 project making semi-permanent blue dyes from blackcurrant skin waste [3]. Forum users ask about the best natural dye [12]. One study tested a gallic acid-based dye in patients who reacted to PPD or PTD [7].

A looksmax.org thread says dye works well on eyebrows, lashes and facial hair for dark-haired users [4], and another poster who was using minoxidil and castor oil around the eye area asked what colour to dye the resulting hair, with a reply suggesting regular brown rather than going too dark [2]. Wikipedia's hair-colouring article records the Egyptian Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BCE) as including recipes for dyeing grey hair and eyebrows [3].

Skin-contact dyes around the eyes and on the face are a point where PPD allergy matters most. The black henna article on Wikipedia describes PPD-containing body-paint pastes that cause blistering, scarring and lifelong sensitivity, and says hair dye labels now warn people who reacted to black henna tattoos not to colour their hair [13].

Wikipedia traces dyeing to Assyrian herbals from about 2177 BCE, the Ebers Papyrus recipes of about 1550 BCE, and Greek historian Diodorus Siculus's description of Celts bleaching hair with lime [3]. Trotula's twelfth-century text and a 1661 compendium of secrets contain colouring recipes [3].

The synthetic era starts in 1856 when William Henry Perkin discovered mauveine while trying to make quinine; the reactivity of PPD in the 1860s underlies later hair dyes; L'Oreal founder Eugene Schueller is credited with the first synthetic hair dye in 1907; and Schwarzkopf launched the first home colour product, Poly Color, in 1947 [3].

PPD-based dyes are the main allergen concern. Reactions include redness, itching, burning and sores, sometimes appearing hours or days later [3]. The Centers for Disease Control lists PPD as a contact allergen, sensitisation is described as lifelong, PPD was the tenth most prevalent patch-test allergen in 2005 to 2006 at 5.0 percent, and the American Contact Dermatitis Society named it Allergen of the Year in 2006, according to Wikipedia [8]. Reviews of cosmetic contact allergy and of dye allergy cover diagnosis and regulation [5][6][14].

Manufacturers usually advise a 48-hour patch test. A multicentre study found the consumer open test, also called the dab test, could detect contact sensitivity to hair dyes [15], while Wikipedia says European dermatologists advise against self-testing because it can itself cause sensitisation [3]. Hairdressers face occupational risk, and a Danish programme followed hairdressing apprentices for hand eczema over six years [16].

Dye can stain skin and nails around the hairline, usually fading within days to a week, and gloves or an oil barrier are recommended on the Wikipedia page [3]. Wikipedia lists hair breakage and unexpected colour results among possible adverse effects [3]. Forum users ask how to minimise damage and one reports greasy-looking hair after dyeing [1].

A 1975 study using a bacterial test found 89 percent of 169 commercial hair dyes mutagenic, a finding often cited in later debate [17]. A 2004 review examined toxicity and human health risk of hair dyes [18]. The National Cancer Institute reports that aromatic amines were removed from products from the mid to late 1970s, that IARC judged some chemicals met by hairdressers and barbers probably carcinogenic in 2010 but classes personal use as not classifiable, that a pooled analysis of 17 studies found no overall bladder cancer increase, and that a 2020 US cohort found higher breast cancer risk with greater exposure (1.07 times among non-Hispanic White women and 1.45 times among Black women) [9].

Wikipedia reports a 2017 meta-analysis suggesting roughly 20 percent higher breast cancer risk among users and notes evidence linking dye to cancer is limited and inconsistent [3]. A Hacker News thread on the 2019 study of permanent dye and chemical straighteners drew 123 points and 43 comments [19].

Wikipedia reports that the EU, through Directive 2012/21/EU under the cosmetics framework, restricts about 45 chemicals in hair dyes, and that some products have been withdrawn over past decades [3]. The black henna article notes that PPD is prohibited on skin in Western countries and that hair dyes may legally contain it only below 6 percent, against 10 to 80 percent found in black henna pastes [13]. An expert panel has published cosmetic ingredient safety assessments of individual hair colorants such as Basic Red 76 [20][14].

A multicentre clinical trial studied a permanent dye containing paratoluenediamine [21], a clinical study tested a gallic acid-based dye in patients reactive to PPD or PTD [7], and a PPD-specific lymphocyte activation test was evaluated in patients with severe allergic reactions [22]. Controlled and observational studies cover hairdressers' hand eczema [16] and the consumer open test [15]. No studies were found on dyeing as a looksmaxxing practice.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, hair dye threads cover colour choice for face and contrast, damage, natural dyes and dye on eyebrows, lashes and facial hair [1][2][4][12][10].
